meta.purpose: Soil-condition-based risk rules for soil-borne diseases (distinct from the weather-based foliar disease rules in diseaseRiskRules.json - this file matches against the farm's own soil test readings: pH, moisture, temperature).
sources: Cornell University Greenhouse Horticulture - Root Rot Diseases factsheet: https://greenhouse.cornell.edu/pests-diseases/disease-factsheets/root-rot-diseases/
University of Minnesota Extension - Fusarium Wilt: https://extension.umn.edu/disease-management/fusarium-wilt
UC Davis Soil Health - Soil-borne diseases: https://soilhealth.ucdavis.edu/soil-challenges/soil-borne-diseases
Washington State University Extension - Soil-borne pathogens
meta.confidenceNote: 'sourced' = specific numbers or thresholds are directly stated in the cited university/FAO source. 'general' = the pathogen-crop link is documented, but exact numeric thresholds are this app's reasonable estimate from broader plant pathology knowledge, not a single cited figure - treat these two as lower confidence than 'sourced' rules.

conditions.note: cool to moderate temperature, waterlogged / poorly drained soil

rules.reason: Pythium thrives in cool, wet, poorly drained soil where anaerobic (low-oxygen) pockets form around roots.
rules.prevention: Improve drainage, avoid overwatering, raise beds in low-lying fields, avoid sowing into waterlogged soil.
rules.source: Cornell University Greenhouse Horticulture, Root Rot Diseases factsheet

conditions.note: wet, poorly drained soil; worse with deep planting

rules.reason: Phytophthora needs standing water or saturated soil to produce the swimming spores that infect roots; poor drainage is the single biggest risk factor.
rules.prevention: Ensure the field drains well after irrigation or rain, avoid deep planting, use raised beds in heavy/clay soil.
rules.source: Cornell University Greenhouse Horticulture, Root Rot Diseases factsheet

conditions.note: intermediate moisture - neither waterlogged nor dry; warm season

rules.reason: Unlike most root-rot fungi, Rhizoctonia is worst in soil that is moderately moist (not fully saturated) and warm - typically a spring/summer problem.
rules.prevention: Avoid both extremes - don't let soil dry out and crust, don't overwater. Rotate with a non-host crop.
rules.source: Cornell University Greenhouse Horticulture, Root Rot Diseases factsheet; UC Davis Soil Health

conditions.note: warm soil (optimal near 28C) and acidic pH

rules.reason: Fusarium wilt gets worse in warm soil (its optimum is around 28C / 82F) and in acidic conditions; disease severity rises as temperature climbs.
rules.prevention: Raising soil pH toward 7 with liming reduces disease severity. Rotate away from susceptible crops, use resistant varieties where available.
rules.source: University of Minnesota Extension, Fusarium Wilt; Washington State University Extension

rules.reason: Bacterial wilt spreads through soil moisture and warm conditions; it is a well-documented risk for solanaceous crops (tomato, potato, chilli, brinjal) in warm, wet fields.
rules.prevention: Improve drainage, avoid working in fields when soil is very wet (spreads the bacteria), rotate with non-host crops, use certified disease-free seed/seedlings.
rules.source: UC Davis Soil Health - Soil Challenges (soil-borne diseases overview)

conditions.note: near-neutral to mildly alkaline pH with poor drainage; largely absent in strongly acidic soil

rules.reason: This disease is specifically pH-linked: it is not a problem when soil is kept acidic (pH 4.5-5.0), but higher pH (6.5-7.0) together with poor drainage encourages it.
rules.prevention: Where this disease has been a problem before, avoid over-liming the soil and improve drainage.
rules.source: Cornell University Greenhouse Horticulture, Root Rot Diseases factsheet

rules.reason: Root-knot nematodes are most active and damaging in warm, sandy, well-aerated soil - the opposite conditions from the fungal root rots above.
rules.prevention: Rotate with non-host crops (e.g. marigold as a trap crop), add organic matter, avoid continuous mono-cropping of susceptible vegetables.
rules.source: General plant nematology consensus (university extension services, e.g. NC State, University of Florida IFAS)
